requirement_summary.summary: Acl destructor must delete all Zone* pointers stored in its entries vector to prevent memory leaks
The std::set mechanism must prevent double-free when the same Zone* appears in multiple ACL entries
After deletion, zone pointers in entries should be set to NULL to prevent dangling pointer access
The entries vector should be cleared after deletion to ensure clean destructor state
The fix must handle NULL zone pointers in entries without crashing
findMostSpecificMatch must return the zone with the longest matching prefix, using last-match tie-breaking for equal prefixes
propagateTSIGKey must not overwrite existing TSIG keys on ACL sub-zones
checkAccess must return the first matching ACL entry (in insertion order) for a client IP
checkAccess must handle NULL out_zone parameter gracefully without crashing

change_clusters.why_it_matters: The entire PR centers on this destructor. MUT-1 proved test_acl_toString catches double-free. MUT-2/3 survived — no test detects memory leaks. Need a different double-free angle.
Longest-prefix-match is core split-horizon DNS logic. Tests use distinct prefix lengths (24,28,30) — tie-breaking with equal lengths is untested.
TSIG key propagation should preserve existing keys. Test only calls propagateTSIGKey once — overwrite-after-first-propagation path is untested.
First-match behavior for overlapping subnets and NULL out_zone safety are untested paths.

mutations.why_this_change_matters: Removes `deleted_zones.insert(it->zone)` but keeps the std::set declaration and the `find()` guard. The set is always empty, so `find()` always returns end(), making the condition always true for any non-NULL pointer. When the same Zone* appears in two entries (as in test_acl_toString), the FIRST encounter deletes the pointer and NULLs the entry; the SECOND encounter sees a non-NULL pointer in the OTHER entry, `find()` returns end() (set was never populated), so `delete` is called again on the already-freed pointer — double-free crash. This tests a DIFFERENT failure mode than MUT-1 (which removed the entire set): here the tracking mechanism exists (the set is declared + find is used) but never populated, so a developer might think it works while it silently fails to track anything.
mutations.original_behavior: After deleting each Zone*, the pointer is inserted into `deleted_zones`, so subsequent encounters of the same pointer find it in the set and skip deletion, preventing double-free.
mutations.mutated_behavior: The `deleted_zones.insert(it->zone)` call is removed. The set is always empty, so every non-NULL Zone* is unconditionally deleted on every encounter. When the same pointer appears in two entries, the second `delete` is a double-free.
mutations.expected_test_signal: SIGSEGV or SIGABRT from test_acl_toString (same zone in two entries causes double-free crash). Should be killed, confirming test_acl_toString also catches this variant.

mutations.why_this_change_matters: Changes `>=` to `>` in the most-specific-match comparison. The current logic uses `>=`, meaning when two ACL entries have the same prefix length, the LAST matching entry wins (it updates `best_match` because `current_mask >= best_mask` is true). With `>`, the FIRST matching entry wins for equal prefix lengths. All existing tests use DISTINCT prefix lengths (24, 28, 30) so this change is invisible. A test with two entries sharing the same prefix length (e.g., two /24 subnets) would expose the difference. This mutation reveals a gap: no test verifies tie-breaking behavior for equal-length prefixes.
mutations.original_behavior: With `>=`: for equal prefix lengths, the last matching ACL entry is returned (later entries override earlier ones at the same specificity).
mutations.mutated_behavior: With `>`: for equal prefix lengths, the first matching ACL entry is returned (earlier entries are preserved, later ones are ignored).
mutations.expected_test_signal: All existing tests pass because they use distinct prefix lengths. New test with equal-length overlapping subnets would detect the difference.
suggested_test_scope: new test: two ACL entries with same /24 prefix but different zones, verify which zone is returned for a matching IP

mutations.why_this_change_matters: Removes the `!it->zone->tsig_key` guard that prevents overwriting existing TSIG keys. Without this guard, calling propagateTSIGKey on a zone that already has a TSIG key will: (1) overwrite the existing key pointer with a new allocation (memory leak of the old key), and (2) change the key unexpectedly. The test test_acl_tsig_propagation only calls propagateTSIGKey ONCE on zones that have no existing key, so the guard is never exercised. This mutation survives, revealing a gap: no test verifies that existing TSIG keys are preserved on re-propagation.
mutations.original_behavior: propagateTSIGKey only assigns a new TSIG::Key if the zone's tsig_key is NULL, preserving existing keys.
mutations.mutated_behavior: propagateTSIGKey unconditionally overwrites it->zone->tsig_key with a new copy, leaking the previous key (if any) and potentially changing the key unexpectedly.
mutations.expected_test_signal: test_acl_tsig_propagation passes because it only propagates once onto zones with no existing key. No test calls propagateTSIGKey twice on the same Acl, so the overwrite path is untested.
suggested_test_scope: new test: propagate TSIG key, change key, propagate again, verify the first key is preserved

mutations.why_this_change_matters: Reverses the iteration direction in checkAccess from forward (first-match wins) to backward (last-match wins). For non-overlapping subnets — like the test's 192.168.1.0/24 and 10.0.0.0/8 — the same IP can never match both, so the iteration direction doesn't change results. However, for overlapping subnets (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.0.0/16 where a single IP could match both), the order determines which zone is returned. No existing test exercises overlapping subnets with checkAccess (findMostSpecificMatch is what's tested for overlaps). This reveals a gap: overlapping-subnet behavior in checkAccess is untested.
mutations.original_behavior: checkAccess iterates forward (begin → end) and returns the FIRST matching entry. For overlapping subnets, the first-added subnet wins.
mutations.mutated_behavior: checkAccess iterates backward (rbegin → rend) and returns the LAST matching entry (the one added most recently). For overlapping subnets, the last-added subnet wins.
mutations.expected_test_signal: All existing tests pass because they use non-overlapping subnets (192.168.1.0/24 vs 10.0.0.0/8). A test with overlapping subnets would detect the difference.
suggested_test_scope: new test: add two entries with overlapping subnets (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.0.0.0/16) with different zones, verify first-added zone is returned

mutations.why_this_change_matters: Removes the `if (out_zone)` guard that prevents null-pointer dereference when checkAccess is called with a NULL out_zone parameter. The presence of this guard indicates the API DESIGN allows callers to pass NULL when they only want the boolean result (access granted/denied) without caring which zone matched. Removing it would crash if any caller passes NULL. All tests pass a valid pointer (`&matched_zone`), so they wouldn't catch this. This reveals a gap: no test calls checkAccess with NULL out_zone to verify the safety guard works.
mutations.original_behavior: When out_zone is NULL, the function skips the `*out_zone = it->zone` assignment and returns the boolean result safely.
mutations.mutated_behavior: The null check is removed; `*out_zone = it->zone` executes unconditionally. If out_zone is NULL, this writes to address NULL, causing a segfault.
mutations.expected_test_signal: All existing tests pass because they always pass &matched_zone (a valid stack pointer). No test exercises NULL out_zone. A new test calling `acl.checkAccess(ip, NULL)` would crash, revealing the guard is needed.
suggested_test_scope: new test: call checkAccess with NULL out_zone, verify it returns true/false without crashing

planner_notes: Round 1 produced 1 killed (MUT-1), 2 real survivors (MUT-2, MUT-3), and 2 equivalent/noop mutants (MUT-4, MUT-5).
CL-1 still has survivors (memory leaks from MUT-2/MUT-3). MUT-6 explores a new angle in the double-free-protection family (remove insert but keep set+find).
New clusters CL-2 (findMostSpecificMatch), CL-3 (propagateTSIGKey), and CL-4 (checkAccess) were introduced to probe untested behavioral paths beyond the destructor.
MUT-7 (>= → > in findMostSpecificMatch) targets tie-breaking logic — tests all use distinct prefix lengths so this is untested.
MUT-8 (remove !tsig_key guard) targets overwrite-on-repropagation — test only propagates once.
MUT-9 (reverse iteration in checkAccess) targets first-match vs last-match for overlapping subnets — tests use disjoint subnet ranges.
MUT-10 (remove out_zone null check) targets NULL parameter safety — no test calls checkAccess with NULL out_zone.
All 5 new mutations compile successfully. MUT-9 has slightly lower compile confidence (0.95) due to iterator type change; others are 0.99.
Total compile failures across both rounds: 0/10 = 0%, well under the 30% threshold. No need to reduce aggressiveness.
